newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's human mole basks in media spotlight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's human mole basks in media spotlight.

text.p: In his mud-stained wellingtons, scruffy trousers and battered anorak, he looks more like a homeless down-and-out than Britain's latest media darling.
But behind the matted hair and grimy fingernails lies Britain's top environmental activist and eco-warrior -- Swampy.
Until recently the 23-year-old former toy shop assistant was just one of dozens of anonymous demonstrators protesting against road projects they say are ruining the environment.
All that changed after he eluded bailiffs for seven days in an elaborate web of tunnels 30 feet (10 metres) under the site of a 30 million pound ($48.2 million) bypass in Devon, southwest England.
He was the last to emerge from his dark, dirty lair, blinking in the blinding sunlight and astonished by the waiting media.

His subterranean protest made national headlines for days. Not only had he delayed the project for a week, hiking costs by an estimated 700,000 pounds ($1.12 million), Swampy, the human mole, had captured the imagination of the nation.
"It felt like a victory. We achieved maximum press coverage, more than we had expected, and it laid the path for the next protest," he said in an interview.
"I think people now fancy us not so much as a bunch of scruffy eco-warriors but as people doing what we're doing. Hopefully that will drive other people to get involved."
NATIONAL CELEBRITY
Since the Devon protest Swampy's cherubic face has appeared in newspapers, magazines and on television.
He has defended his tactics on TV chat shows, writes a column for a Sunday newspaper and even submitted to a temporary makeover, complete with Giorgio Armani suit.
His cheeky grin is more familiar to Britons than the faces of some cabinet ministers. Despite what could have proved to be a lucrative deal, he turned down a recording contract.
"They wanted us to do 'Mole in the Hole' by Swampy and the Swampettes," he said with a smirk.
Instead, he is devoting his time to a new project, blocking the construction of a second runway at Manchester airport in northern England.

"I went to Manchester and saw how much of the land it was trashing. I saw the lay of the land and realised we had an amazingly defendable place and it's definitely a cause worth fighting for. It is 550 hectares (1,359 acres) of beautiful landscape -- apart from the airport next store."

Up to 40 protesters have already set up camps in treehouses surrounding the airport site. Swampy and his colleagues have dug four or five tunnels and are promising to make their latest cause bigger, better and longer than the Devon protest.
DIRECT ACTION POPULAR FORM OF PROTEST

Direct, non-violent action has become an increasingly popular form of protest by young Britons. Anti-road protesters learned useful lessons during lengthy, unsuccessful battles to stop projects at Twyford Down and Newbury in southern Britain and they proved more than a match for officialdom in Devon.
The army, 100 police and up to 300 security officers took part in the Devon eviction, removing people with great difficulty from well-protected tree houses and tunnels.
Swampy, so named because he is usually the dirtiest and wettest of the protesters, was the last of five tunnellers to emerge from "Big Mama", the intricate network of caves and chambers they built.

Even a crew of mysterious men wearing black balaclavas, believed to be ex-military, who were sent into the tunnels to prepare the way for the bailiffs, seemed to have had a sneaking admiration for the human moles.
"They were nice people. We got on all right. There wasn't much aggression," Swampy said of his masked opponents.
Thanks to the experience he gained in Devon, where the narrow tunnels zigzagged to thwart the bailiffs, Swampy says he has a few new tricks up his sleeve to prolong the Manchester protest.
He says he is not bothered by the prospect of another week or more in an underground home, eating tinned food and reading by candlelight to stave off the endless hours of boredom.
Nor is he frightened by official warnings that his life could be endangered by methane gas on the site, or the prospect of being arrested and jailed.

By his own estimate he has already been arrested seven times. His last court appearance for his Devon escapade saw him hogging the headlines again and an anonymous benefactor sent him 100 pounds ($160) to cover the cost of any fine.
To the cheers of his supporters he received only a conditional discharge, and promised to put the 100 pounds towards the cost of a drill for the Manchester runway protest.
Turning the tables on his accusers, he said the people who are wrecking the environment should have been in court, not him.

"We're just everyday people trying to protect the environment. We're not necessarily poor or rich. It's all different kinds of people getting together to say 'Enough, we're not going to put up with the environmental damage anymore. We won't let the planet be destroyed'.
"It's getting to the point where, if we don't change soon, there is not going to be anything left to change and it will be too late." ($1=.6228 Pound)
